name: keras
title: Keras: A Multi-Backend Deep Learning Framework for AI
answer: Keras is an open-source Python library for building and training deep learning models, now in its 3.0 release with support for JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, and OpenVINO backends. It sits at the model-definition and training layer of the AI stack, offering high-level APIs like Sequential, Functional, and subclassing. The one thing to know: Keras 3 lets you write one model and run it across multiple frameworks, but performance varies by backend and model.

sections.body: Keras is an open-source deep learning library written in Python, maintained by the Keras team and released under the Apache 2.0 license. It first appeared in 2015 as a high-level interface for neural networks and has since evolved into a multi-backend framework. With Keras 3.0, officially released and documented on keras.io, it can run on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO for inference. It occupies the model-building and training layer of the AI stack, providing abstractions for layers, models, metrics, losses, optimizers, and training loops. It is not a low-level tensor library or a data processing engine, but a cross-framework language for defining and training models.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: Keras is used for the full range of deep learning tasks: training, evaluation, inference, and data preprocessing. Its built-in methods like fit(), evaluate(), and predict() work uniformly across Sequential models, Functional API models, and subclassed models. It supports image classification, text generation, autoencoders, transfer learning, and more, as shown in official examples such as a mini-GPT for text generation and a sample size estimation recipe for medical imaging. It is strongest when you want a clean, high-level API that works across backends, and when you need to move between experimentation and production without rewriting code. It is also well suited for custom components like layers and metrics that can be shared across JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: Keras is designed to be approachable for beginners, with a consistent API and extensive guides on keras.io covering Sequential models, the Functional API, and built-in training methods. However, to use it effectively you need a basic understanding of neural network concepts such as layers, loss functions, optimizers, and metrics, as well as familiarity with Python and NumPy arrays. For advanced use, such as custom training loops or distribution, you may need deeper knowledge of the chosen backend, for example JAX or TensorFlow. The official site offers step-by-step examples, API references, and guides that start from loading data and building a simple model, making it accessible for students and developers new to deep learning.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: Keras has a large ecosystem, with over 64,000 stars on GitHub and adoption by more than 2.5 million developers according to the Keras 3 announcement. It integrates with KerasHub for pretrained models and layers, and supports data pipelines from NumPy arrays, tf.data.Dataset, PyTorch DataLoader, and Pandas dataframes. The keras.ops namespace provides a backend-agnostic set of operations, and the keras.distribution API (currently for JAX) enables model and data parallelism. Documentation on keras.io includes guides, examples, and API references. The community is active, with contributions to the core repository and a wide range of third-party tutorials and projects.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Keras is built for both quick experiments and production deployment. Its high-level APIs like Sequential and Functional allow rapid prototyping, while the ability to switch backends means you can train on JAX for speed and deploy on TensorFlow or PyTorch for integration. Benchmarks cited in the Keras 3 announcement show JAX typically delivers the best training and inference performance on GPU, TPU, and CPU, though results vary by model, and non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU. The cost is that you may need to tune backend-specific settings for optimal performance, and some advanced features like the distribution API are not yet available on all backends. For most users, the trade-off is a consistent API and portability against the need to understand backend nuances.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: Keras is used by a wide range of organizations, including Waymo for its self-driving fleet and YouTube for its recommendation engine, as stated on the Keras 3 page. It is a current standard for deep learning development, especially in teams that value flexibility across backends. For someone choosing it for work, Keras skills are transferable because the same code can run on JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch, making it a valuable addition to a resume. However, the official material does not provide detailed adoption statistics beyond the 2.5 million developers figure, so it is not possible to say precisely how it compares to other frameworks in every industry. It is not a legacy choice; it is actively developed, with the last push to the repository in October 2026.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Keras is typically used with Python and integrates with JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch as backends. It can be used as a low-level cross-framework language to develop custom components that work in native workflows in those frameworks. The polyglot pattern it belongs to is one where a high-level API abstracts over multiple lower-level engines, allowing developers to write once and run anywhere. It also works with OpenVINO for inference-only deployments. In practice, you might use Keras for model definition and training, then export to TensorFlow SavedModel or instantiate as a PyTorch Module for serving. This makes it a central piece in a multi-framework AI stack, rather than a replacement for the backends themselves.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: Keras is not ideal for every scenario. The Sequential model is only appropriate for plain stacks of layers with one input and one output tensor, and is not suitable for non-linear topology like residual connections or multi-branch models. The distribution API is currently implemented only for the JAX backend, with TensorFlow and PyTorch support coming soon, so distributed training on those backends may require other tools. The official material does not specify the exact performance overhead of the multi-backend abstraction, nor does it detail memory management or low-level optimization capabilities compared to using a backend directly. It also does not provide a clear comparison of Keras against other high-level APIs in terms of features or community size. These are open questions for a developer evaluating it for a specific production constraint.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
